senses: bumbling; inept or clumsy
To remove from an official register or list.
examples: When the company failed to file its financial statements, it was delisted by the Stock Exchange.
When the property had failed to sell for months on end, it was delisted by the owner, who will try again next spring.

senses: An open shed for sheltering cattle, or protecting produce, etc., from the weather.
In the manufacture of porcelain, a large, conical brick structure around which the firing kilns are grouped.
ety: From Middle English hovel, hovil, hovylle, diminutive of *hove, *hof (“structure, building, house”), from Old English hof (“an enclosure, court, dwelling, house”), from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą (“hill, farm”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“arch, bend, buckle”), equivalent to howf + -el. Compare Middle High German hobel (“cover, lid, covered wagon”). Cognate with Dutch hof (“garden, court”), German Hof (“yard, garden, court, palace”), Icelandic hof (“temple, hall”). Related to hove and hover.

senses: A tree, Paullinia cupana, native to Venezuela and northern Brazil.
The fruit from this tree, chiefly used to make caffeinated beverages.
An edible paste prepared from the seeds of the tree, formed into round or oblong cakes.
ety: From Brazilian Portuguese guaraná, from Sateré-Mawé warana.

senses: Transhumanism or a similar philosophy.
Having a shore, often one of a specified type.
The amount or level of dissolved carbon dioxide remaining in solution.
Synonym of carbonization.
examples: Celia didn't eat at the diner anymore because she thought the carbonation in their fountain drinks was off.

senses: A children's game in which the players hide together, lying side by side.
ety: The game name refers to sardines tightly packed in a can.

senses: A traditional Kenyan community self-help event or organization.
examples: The tension between spontaneity and control, which is at the core of nearly all analyses of harambee, is usually supposed to be that between the contending forces of 'the people' and the state.

senses: To furnish with an addendum.
ety: Short for addendum, by surface analysis, add + -end.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a seal (the animal).
examples: If you reply that, on the contrary, the seal's legs, such as they are, are very characteristic, he takes refuge in the atrocious admission, delivered with a French accent, that they are certainly very sealy legs.

senses: The title of the hereditary monarch of Egypt from 1805–1914, nominally ruling as a viceroy of the Sultan of Turkey.
ety: From French khédive, from Ottoman Turkish خدیو (ḫediv, ḫıdiv), from Persian خدیو (xadêw, xedêw, “lord, master, king”), from Bactrian χοαδηο (khoadēo, “lord”).

senses: Any of a pair of confocal mirrors or lenses
A mop, especially one used to clean a baker's oven.
ety: From Malde, an early form of Maude or Matilda + -kin (diminutive ending). Compare grimalkin.

senses: Synonym of gigantism.
ety: From giant + -ism, coined in the mid 17th century. In the medical or biological sense of gigantism from the 1880s.

senses: Full of sheltered hollows or recesses.
Having a large bosom.
Being or relating to a kind of tube socket base having eight pins.
Any of genera Acanthostracion and Lactoria, of the boxfish family Ostraciidae.
A grampus (Grampus griseus), Risso's dolphin.
A common bottlenose dolphin of California, Tursiops truncatus gillii.
A common galaxias (Galaxias maculatus)
Producing new ideas or products.
Involving killing.
That which decouples.
UK standard spelling of pedophilic.
A piezoelectric material or device.
The time, or the condition, of budding or flowering.
ety: From Latin florēscō, from flōreō (“to bloom, flower”) + -ēscō, from flōs (“flower”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”), as if through the form flōrēscentia.

senses: mincing; affectedly dainty
An inclination; a cant.
A decline; decrease; wane.
ety: From Middle English held, from Old English hielde (“slope, declivity”), from Proto-Germanic *halþijōn, *halþijō (“inclination, slope”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to tilt, tip, incline”). Cognate with German Halde (“slope”), Danish hæld (“an incline, slope”).

senses: To set with bright points: star or spangle.
To hitch; fasten.
ety: From Middle English spang (“a small piece of ornamental metal; spangle; small ornament; a bowl or cup”), likely from Middle Dutch spange (“buckle, clasp”) or Old English spang (“buckle, clasp”).

senses: A composition that is playful in attitude and tone.
A revolving circular plate, set obliquely on its shaft, and acting as a cam to give a reciprocating motion to a rod in a direction parallel to the shaft.
A device that translates input from a helicopter's controls into motion of the main rotor blades.
Full of roots.
Resembling or characteristic of roots.
examples: Disk plows also are better suited to rough, stony, and rooty ground because the disks ride over the obstructions.
The vegetable stew had an earthy, rooty flavour.

senses: To remove a tag from.
A bone shaped like an elongated barbell.
Any object with such a shape.
ety: From dog + bone. Evokes a bone to be given to a dog to chew on, rather the bone of a dog.

senses: A type of wagashi that contains very little moisture and thus keeps relatively longer than other kinds.
ety: From Japanese 干菓子 /乾菓子 (higashi, literally “dry confectionery”).

senses: The emergence of a distinct, recognizable, ethnic identity.
ety: From ethno- + -genesis. While attested incidentally before the twentieth century, it gained currency particularly in the postwar era as a scholarly concept.

senses: A very powerful mage.
Such a system
Any substance undergoing analysis.
Serving as a token of support, compliance, etc., but lacking substance; exhibiting or relating to tokenism.
examples: The government has taken nothing more than tokenistic actions on behalf of people with disabilities.
The company’s use of ads depicting gay couples appears to be merely tokenistic, particularly in view of the support it has given to anti-LGBT politicians.
But what is not needed is a tokenistic gesture to place a woman, any woman, in the role, irrespective of her politics.

senses: Flowing out; outflowing.
ety: From French effluent, from Latin effluens, effluentis. By surface analysis, e- + fluent.

senses: barons or nobles collectively
an annotated list of barons or peers
ety: From Middle English barnage, from Old French (and Anglo-Norman) barnage, from baron + -age, with the loss of a syllable.
